paras: The Rockingham registration fight was an attack by a large party of white men on a revenue officer named Spears and about 100 Black men he had brought to register as voters at Rockingham, North Carolina, on election day, November 7, 1882. Spears was badly beaten and several of the Black men were severely injured, and many arrests were reported.

Spears, described as a revenue officer or 'government employee', came into Rockingham with a party of a hundred or more Black men and took them before the registrar to have their names entered. According to the Charlotte Observer, the registrar refused because the men 'were not residents of that township', and Spears insisted while the registrar held firm.

A wire dispatch dated Rockingham, November 7, said the party was 'attacked by a large party of white men and driven from the polling places' that morning, with Spears badly beaten and several Black men severely injured. The Charlotte Observer placed the clash at about three in the afternoon and called it 'a big fight'.
The wire reported that 'the greatest excitement prevails and many arrests are being made'; no names, charges or later proceedings appear in the coverage.

The Augusta, Maine, Daily Kennebec Journal printed the wire on November 8 under a plain 'North Carolina' head beside election returns, calling Spears's party 'a mob of over 100 negroes'. The Springfield Weekly Republican, citing a private dispatch to the Republican national committee, ran it under 'Trouble at the Polls' and reversed the label: 'A mob of whites fell on them, by way of reply'.

The Weekly Union Times of Union Court House, South Carolina, reprinted the Charlotte Observer's item under the head 'A Fight Between Citizens and Negroes', giving the registrar's residency objection and describing a 'riot between whites and blacks' without naming an aggressor.

Where the wire and the Republican have whites attacking, the Charlotte Observer describes a mutual fight; it also names Spears 'F. S.' rather than 'O. J.', and its credit to the issue of the '5th' would date the fight to November 4.

reader.title: Rockingham registration fight (1882)
bases: A large party of white men attacked and beat a revenue officer and the Black men he brought to register, injuring several, with no deaths reported (A1, A2, A3).

A wire dispatch (A1), a private dispatch to the Republican national committee (A2) and the Charlotte Observer (A3) agree that Spears brought about 100 Black men to register at Rockingham and that he and several of them were badly hurt in a fight with whites, though they differ on who started it.

accounts.label: Rockingham wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Spears 'led a mob of over 100 negroes' into town that morning to demand registration; a large party of white men attacked and drove them from the polls, beating Spears and severely injuring several Black men; many arrests followed.

accounts.label: Private dispatch to the Republican national committee
accounts.gist: Spears led 100 Black men into Rockingham on Tuesday to register; 'A mob of whites fell on them', beating Spears and hurting several; many arrests were made.

accounts.label: Charlotte Observer
accounts.gist: About 3 p.m. Spears brought a hundred or more Black men before the registrar, who refused them as non-residents of the township; Spears insisted and 'a big fight' followed in which he and several Black men were 'badly used up'.

framing.detail: The Kennebec Journal printed the wire under a plain 'North Carolina' head, calling the Black men 'a mob' while also saying the white party 'attacked' them.

The Republican placed the item under 'Trouble at the Polls' beside a 'red shirts' killing in South Carolina, called the whites 'A mob' and said they answered the registration demand 'by way of reply' with a beating.

The Charlotte Observer, reprinted in South Carolina, headlined 'A Fight Between Citizens and Negroes', gave the registrar's reason for refusal, and described a mutual 'riot' without naming an aggressor.
